\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to $\leq$\,0.21\% at F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp vs.\ unconstrained), converting irrecoverable type errors to correctable cross-field inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B at ${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency.
97.6--100\% of enforcement-removed triples are false positives.
In zero-shot settings, DR reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; CF increases are concentrated in hallucinated entities (58.1\%) and decrease with scale and fine-tuning.
\end{abstract}

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%---the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.
On DocRED (96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$), grammar-only \emph{increases} DR via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: forcing OOV$\to$valid relation mapping exposes violations previously masked by vocabulary errors (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Cross-model validation (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}) confirms DR drops of 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with R-F1 improving in 5/6 settings; post-hoc filtering achieves DR${=}$0\% but at 15--74\% rejection rates.
DR-to-CF conversion represents a severity downgrade: DR is irrecoverable without re-extraction, while CF---individually valid triples with cross-triple inconsistency---is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR eliminates all CF in our experiments, with bounded DR regression; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
Zero-shot evaluation thus establishes violation prevalence and constraint interaction; fine-tuning demonstrates practical elimination.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (e) Composability with Fine-Tuning (expanded)
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).
Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (41--69\% on SciERC, 2--75\% on DocRED; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).
Fallback frequency is model-dependent: Qwen triggers 0 fallbacks under LoRA + S1 on SciERC, while Llama triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), reflecting weaker entity typing; despite this, DR reaches 0.09\% on SciERC (0.21\% on DocRED), confirming that even frequent fallback does not compromise enforcement.
CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\% of zero-shot CF; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  CF quantification (MF1 response)

\paragraph{Cross-field violation analysis.}
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (ZS: CF=248, 167 docs), w5_lora_scierc_full_s1_eval (FT: CF=22, 20 docs)
Under zero-shot greedy S1, CF is the sole residual violation type (DR, RV, ET all eliminated): 248 cross-field violations arise across 167 documents, of which 63.3\% involve \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X type ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{OtherScientificTerm} (34.7\%) and \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\textsc{Material} (12.3\%).
A source breakdown (Appendix~\ref{app:cascade-analysis}) shows 58.1\% originate from hallucinated entities (a model capacity issue), while true cascade errors---where first-seen registration locks an incorrect type---account for only 7.3\%; correct locks are 2.5$\times$ more frequent, confirming first-seen registration as a net-positive mechanism.
Fine-tuning reduces CF to 22 cross-field violation instances across 20 documents (1.18\%), with cascade errors completely eliminated (0/22).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all remaining CF at 1.39$\times$ latency (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

DocRED (96 relations, 14$\times$ SciERC scale) validates the pattern under a larger, more restrictive ontology (Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation}).
S1 reduces DR from 18.46\% to 10.21\% ($\downarrow$45\%), eliminates RV (29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%) and ET, with R-F1 $+$0.49\,pp ($p < 0.001$).
The lower DR reduction (45\% vs.\ 94\% on SciERC) reflects DocRED's tighter constraints, which trigger more grammar-first fallback (\S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}).
Grammar-only \emph{increases} DR (18.46\%\,$\to$\,26.17\%) via \textit{latent violation surfacing}: grammar forces OOV$\to$valid relation mapping, exposing type violations previously masked by vocabulary errors---a distinct cross-dataset confirmation of the empirical enabling dependency.
Fine-tuning reduces residual DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% (Table~\ref{tab:composability}; residual decomposition in Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

file.content:
% §5 Setup (compressed from Violation Landscape)
% exp_ids: mvp_phase0_violation_rate, mvp_phase0_scierc_schema,
%          mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred, mvp_phase0_docred_schema

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations: greedy S1 (DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, $+$10\% latency) and beam S1 (all violations\,$\to$\,0\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}) serves as a diagnostic probe for the fine-tuned setting (R-F1 40--46\%).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 development documents; test annotations are not publicly available; 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) derive from the KAIROS ontology.
All constraints are schema-level, independent of evaluation splits.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
LoRA hyperparameters (rank, $\alpha$, learning rate) were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization; given the substantial schema complexity difference (7 vs.\ 96 relations), this transfer may underestimate DocRED fine-tuning potential.
Our R-F1 range (40--46\% under LoRA) is consistent with recent LLM-based generative RE evaluations on these benchmarks, where document-level closed IE without gold entity spans typically achieves 35--50\%~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}; supervised span-based methods operating under different assumptions (gold entity spans, dedicated architectures) are not directly comparable.
For reference, the supervised end-to-end SOTA on SciERC achieves 41.6\% strict Rel-F1 (PL-Marker~\cite{ye2022packed}) and 36.8\% (PURE~\cite{zhong2021frustratingly}); while evaluation protocols differ, our 40--46\% R-F1 range under LoRA falls within a comparable band.
DocRED development documents were used for evaluation only.
Four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), \textbf{CF} (conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR: 15.37\% (SciERC), 18.46\% (DocRED); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (${\sim}$1.5$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations (DR+CF) decreasing 30--51\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item An empirical finding of non-additive layer interaction: grammar-only constraints reduce domain-range violations by 3\% and semantic-only by 24\%, but their composition achieves 94\%---revealing an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework showing that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Evidence of scale-dependent layer interaction on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4): the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

The large discrepancy is primarily a tokenization artifact: SciERC entity types are multi-token (e.g., \textsc{OtherScientificTerm}, averaging 2.87 mask calls per type field), and continuation tokens necessarily conflict with the semantic mask, inflating the per-mask-call fallback rate.

CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\% of zero-shot CF; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot diagnostic.}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} establishes that DR violations are pervasive (15--18\% across datasets) and that constraint layers interact non-additively: grammar-only achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic-only 24\%, but their composition yields 94\%---the \emph{empirical enabling dependency}.

% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (f) Downstream impact of DR elimination
%  exp_ids: task_e_lucky_violation_analysis
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Downstream impact.}
\label{sec:downstream-impact}
Constraint removal affects only 0.24\% of gold triples (Appendix~\ref{app:lucky-violations}); error analysis of 514 false negatives confirms only one (0.2\%) was blocked by constraints, with dominant sources (relation confusion, entity type polysemy) schema-valid and beyond constraint reach (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Across fine-tuned settings, 36 residual DR violations decompose into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and relation/direction errors (28\%); the irreducible floor is $\sim$3 violations (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).

lines: \paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
% exp_ids: bootstrap_ci_ft_composability.json, w5_lora_scierc_*, w8_*

-Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).

+Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 0.5--2\% but leaves residual violations on tight-constraint relations (Table~\ref{tab:composability}); adding S1 yields DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% with no significant $\Delta$R-F1 (Bonferroni-corrected; 95\% CIs $\subseteq [-0.69, {+}0.25]$\,pp; removed triples are 97.6--100\% false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream-impact}).

Under fine-tuning, grammar becomes a no-op ($\Delta$DR$<$0.2\,pp), making the semantic layer the sole DR defense (41--69\% on SciERC, 2--75\% on DocRED; Appendix~\ref{app:ft-ablation}); three relations with $\kappa \geq 0.36$ retain DR, all eliminated by S1 (Appendix~\ref{app:lora-per-relation}).

Fallback frequency is model-dependent: Qwen triggers 0 fallbacks under LoRA + S1 on SciERC, while Llama triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), reflecting weaker entity typing; despite this, DR reaches 0.09\% on SciERC (0.21\% on DocRED), confirming that even frequent fallback does not compromise enforcement.

CF drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), concentrated in \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (63.3\% of zero-shot CF; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B (R-F1 43--46; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
